heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji I.ii.14 … Za Ji I.ii.31

items.text: Bury the spirit-tablet after the sacrifice of Repose.
items.quote: The spirit-tablet (which had been set up over the coffin) was buried after the sacrifice of Repose.
items.conflict: Spirit tablets for the dead (Lev 26:1; Deut 18:10-12)

items.text: Give her mourning rites according to your rank.
items.quote: (The mourning rites for) all wives were according to the rank of their husbands.

items.text: Greet and bow to visitors who arrive during the dressing of the corpse and the opening of the coffin.
items.quote: Visitors who had arrived during the slighter dressing... were all saluted and bowed to.

items.text: Do not use women's dress when dressing a male corpse.
items.quote: Zang-dze said, 'In such a dressing there should be nothing of woman's dress.'

items.text: Call back his soul only if he died in a public place, not in a private hotel.
items.quote: if the death took place in a public hotel, they called his soul back; if in a private hotel, they did not do so.
items.conflict: Calling back the soul of the dead (Deut 18:10-12)

items.text: Take part in the prescribed leaping for the deceased for the number of days according to his rank.
items.quote: The women take their share in this expression of grief at intervals.

items.text: Wear the band of sackcloth about your head at the slight dressing of the corpse.
items.quote: At the slight dressing of the corpse the son (or the presiding mourner) wore the band of sackcloth about his head.

heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji II.ii.16 … Za Ji II.ii.32

items.text: When your father or mother dies, return to your original home and perform the ceremonies of condolence.
items.quote: On that occasion she did so, and went back to her original home, where she used the ceremonies of condolence proper to a feudal lord

items.text: Do not lay the soothing hand on the corpse of your brother-in-law or sister-in-law.
items.quote: A sister-in-law did not lay the soothing hand on the corpse of her brother-in-law; and vice versâ.

items.text: Do not encroach on the observances of those above you.
items.quote: A superior man will not encroach on (the observances of) those above him

items.text: Do not put difficulties in the way of those below you.
items.quote: nor put difficulties in the way of those below him

items.text: In bad years, use the lowest victims in your sacrifices.
items.quote: In bad years they used in their sacrifices the victims lowest (in the classes belonging to them).
items.conflict: Ancestor veneration conflicts with Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:10-12; 1 Timothy 2:5.

items.text: Offer the sacrifice in the temple to all the progenitors of your line in the seventh month.
items.quote: Accordingly Hsien-dze offered that sacrifice to all the progenitors (of the line of Lû) in the seventh month
items.conflict: Ancestor veneration conflicts with Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:10-12; 1 Timothy 2:5.

heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji I.i.1 … Za Ji I.i.21

items.text: Wear mourning appropriate to your father's rank as a Great officer.
items.quote: The son of a Great officer by his wife proper wore the mourning appropriate for a Great officer.

items.text: If your father was a Great officer and you are his son by a concubine but also a Great officer, wear mourning for him as for a Great officer.
items.quote: The son of a Great officer by any other member of his harem, who was himself a Great officer wore for his father or mother the mourning of a Great officer.

items.text: If your father has risen above his own parents in rank, you as his son must preside over his mourning rites.
items.quote: They made his son do so; and if he had no son, they appointed some one to perform that part.

items.text: At your father's funeral, after the horses are brought out, fold up the offerings and read the list of gifts.
items.quote: After this (the son) folded up the offerings, and read the list (of the gifts that had been sent).

items.text: Call back your wife's soul using the robe appropriate to her rank.
items.quote: (In calling back the soul of) a friends wife, they used the black upper robe with a purple border.
items.conflict: Calling back the soul is necromancy; the dead cannot be summoned (Deut. 18:10-12).

items.text: When a cousin dies, wear mourning appropriate to his rank.
items.quote: In the mourning for a cousin... a Great officer wore the mourning appropriate for an ordinary officer; and an ordinary officer... wore the same mourning.

items.text: Place the spirit tablet of a deceased grandson in the shrine according to the prescribed order, based on his rank relative to his grandfather.
items.quote: (The tablet of a grandson who had been) a Great officer was placed (in the shrine of his grandfather who had (only) been an officer; but not if he had only been an officer, and the grandfather a Great officer.
items.conflict: Ancestral tablets are not commanded in Scripture; worship is due to God alone (Exod. 20:4-5).

heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji II.ii.33 … Za Ji II.ii.38

items.text: When divorcing, follow the proper ceremony: send a messenger to convey the message of dismissal.
items.quote: The messenger, accompanying her, then discharged his commission.
items.conflict: Divorce permitted only for adultery (Matthew 19:9); this ceremony treats divorce as routine.

items.text: When departing after divorce, send a messenger to take leave before going.
items.quote: When the wife went away from her husband, she sent a messenger and took leave of him.
items.conflict: Divorce permitted only for adultery (Matthew 19:9); this ceremony treats divorce as routine.

items.text: When a divorced wife returns to her own state, receive her with the honors due to her former rank.
items.quote: When a feudal lord sent his wife away, she proceeded on her journey to her own state, and was received there with the observances due to a lord's wife.

items.text: On first entering the family, present herself for the initial interview with her father-in-law and mother-in-law.
items.quote: At the (first) interview of a wife with her father and mother-in-law...

items.text: After the interview with her parents-in-law, visit each of her husband's married uncles in their own apartments.
items.quote: After this interview, she visited all the married uncles of her husband, each in his own apartment.

items.text: When a daughter reaches maturity, the mother should manage the hair-pin ceremony for her.
items.quote: The (principal) wife managed the ceremony.

heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji II.i.39 … Za Ji II.ii.15

items.text: Preserve your health and do not emaciate yourself to illness or death, for that fails the duty of a son.
items.quote: A superior man will not emaciate himself so as to be ill. If one die from such emaciation, a superior man will say of him that he has failed in the duty of a son.

items.text: In speaking, avoid using the personal names of your paternal grandparents, father's brothers, and father's sisters; in the house avoid names your mother avoids, and by your wife's side avoid names she avoids.
items.quote: (An officer) did not use the name of his (paternal) grandfather or grandmother, of his father's brothers or uncles; of his father's aunts or sisters.

items.text: While your father mourns, keep away from all music; while your mother mourns, you may listen to music but not play it yourself.
items.quote: When the father was wearing mourning, a son, who lived in the same house with him, kept away from all music. When the mother was wearing it, the son might listen to music, but not play himself.

items.text: Do not play music by her side while your wife is in mourning.
items.quote: When a wife was wearing it, the son, (her husband), did not play music by her side.

items.text: If a married woman dies childless and widowed, let a relative of her late husband, however distant, preside at her mourning rites, not any of her own relatives.
items.quote: When an aunt or sister died (leaving no son), if her husband (also) were dead, and there were no brother or cousin in his relative circle, some other of her husband's more distant relatives was employed to preside at her mourning rites.

heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji II.i.6 … Za Ji II.i.22

items.text: When your father or mother dies while you are bound to attend a ruler’s sacrifice, complete the sacrifice, then put off sacrificial dress, go outside the palace gate, wail, and return home to proceed with mourning.
items.quote: if his father or mother died... After the sacrifice he put off his (sacrificial) dress, went outside the gate of the palace, wailed, and returned to his own house.

items.text: If an uncle, aunt, or cousin dies when you have already received notice to fast, attend the ruler’s sacrifice, then put off your sacrificial dress and go home to mourn; if the deceased lived with you, take up residence in another apartment.
items.quote: uncle, aunt, or cousin... put off his sacrificial dress, and returned... If they lived under the same roof, he took up his residence in other apartments.

items.text: When mourning a parent, if a brother or cousin dies, postpone the sacrifice for the parent until that relative is buried.
items.quote: During the mourning rites for a parent... if a death occurred in the family of a brother or cousin, the sacrifice was postponed till the burial of the dead had taken place.

items.text: In mourning your parents, let reverence be most important, grief next, and emaciation last; let your face show your inward feeling and your demeanor match your dress.
items.quote: Reverence is the most important thing; grief is next to it; and emaciation is the last. The face should wear the appearance of the inward feeling.

items.text: During the three years of mourning for a father, dwell alone in the hut or unplastered room, speak but do not discourse, reply but do not ask, and do not enter the main house except to appear before your mother.
items.quote: might speak, but did not discourse; might reply, but did not ask questions... unless there were some occasion for him to appear before his mother, he did not enter the door.

items.text: Mourn your wife with grief equal to that for an uncle or aunt.
items.quote: The grief in mourning for a wife was like that for an uncle or aunt.

items.text: Even after the three-year external mourning for parents is over, continue to mourn them inwardly.
items.quote: The mourning for parents is taken away (at the end of three years), (but only) its external symbols.

items.text: After one year of mourning for a brother, cease mourning both outwardly and inwardly.
items.quote: the mourning for brothers (at the end of one year), (and also) internally.

heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji I.i.22 … Za Ji I.ii.13

items.text: Place the tablet of a deceased wife after that of the principal wife in her husband's shrine, or in the shrine of the high ancestor's wife if there is none.
items.quote: The (tablet of a) wife was placed after that of the wife (of the principal of the shrine), in which her husband's tablet was placed.
items.conflict: Ancestor tablets and sacrifices conflict with the first commandment and Deut. 18:11.

items.text: Place the tablet of a deceased concubine in the shrine of her husband's grandmother concubine, or in that of the high ancestor's concubine if there is none.
items.quote: The (tablet of a) concubine was placed in the shrine of her husband's grandmother (concubine).
items.conflict: Ancestor tablets and sacrifices conflict with the first commandment and Deut. 18:11.

items.text: Place the tablet of an unmarried son in the shrine of his grandfather and use it at sacrifices.
items.quote: The (tablet of) an unmarried son was placed in the shrine of his grandfather, and was used at sacrifices.
items.conflict: Ancestor tablets and sacrifices conflict with the first commandment and Deut. 18:11.

items.text: Place the tablet of an unmarried daughter in the shrine of her grandmother, but do not use it at sacrifices.
items.quote: That of an unmarried daughter was placed in the shrine of her grandmother, but was not used at sacrifices.
items.conflict: Ancestor tablets and sacrifices conflict with the first commandment and Deut. 18:11.

items.text: Place the tablet of a ruler's son in the shrine of a son of his grandfather, if the grandfather was also a ruler.
items.quote: The (tablet of) the son of a ruler was placed in the shrine of (one of) the sons (of his grandfather), that grandfather having also been a ruler.
items.conflict: Ancestor tablets and sacrifices conflict with the first commandment and Deut. 18:11.

items.text: When a brother dies, put on sackcloth and the girdle with dishevelled edges, and coordinate your mourning period with the presiding mourner.
items.quote: His first step then was to put on the sackcloth, and the girdle with dishevelled edges.

items.text: As master, conduct yourself the placing of a concubine's tablet in its proper shrine.
items.quote: The master, presiding at the mourning rites for a concubine, himself conducted the placing of her tablet (in its proper shrine).
items.conflict: Ancestor tablets and sacrifices conflict with the first commandment and Deut. 18:11.

items.text: Preside at the sacrifices at the end of the first and second years for your departed mother (a concubine).
items.quote: At the sacrifices at the end of the first and second years, he employed her son to preside at them.
items.conflict: Ancestor tablets and sacrifices conflict with the first commandment and Deut. 18:11.

items.text: Do not stroke the corpse of a servant or a concubine.
items.quote: A ruler did not stroke the corpse of a servant or a concubine.

items.text: Wail, attend the funeral, and present the sacrifice of Repose for a deceased cousin.
items.quote: The president at the mourning rites for a cousin, though the relationship might not have been near, also presented the sacrifice of Repose.
items.conflict: Sacrifice of Repose to the dead conflicts with the first commandment.

items.text: When mourning for your wife, if your parents are alive, do not carry a staff or bow to the ground; defer to them.
items.quote: (An eldest son), going to wail for his wife, if his parents were alive, did not carry a staff, nor bow so as to lay his forehead on the ground.

items.text: At sacrifices after Repose, call yourself 'the filial son' or 'the filial grandson'; at previous rites, 'the grieving son' or 'the grieving grandson.'
items.quote: At the sacrifices (after the sacrifice of Repose), the mourner styled himself 'The filial son,' or 'The filial grandson;'
items.conflict: Ancestor tablets and sacrifices conflict with the first commandment and Deut. 18:11.

heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji I.ii.32 … Za Ji II.i.5

items.text: Receive funeral gifts sent for the deceased with deep reverence: bow to the messenger and place the items by the coffin.
items.quote: The son bowed to him, with his forehead to the ground; and when the bearer laid down the things on the east of the coffin

items.text: When the ruler sends a representative to wail, receive him with bows, wail and leap with him, and escort him out.
items.quote: The orphaned mourner descended by the steps on the east, and bowed to him, after which they both ascended and wailed

items.text: When the corpse is dressed, kneel facing east, lean on the coffin, and leap.
items.quote: The wife with her face to the east, also leant on it, kneeling; and then she got up and leaped.

items.text: When the corpse is dressed, lean on the coffin and leap.
items.quote: The son then leant on the coffin and leaped.

items.text: If your mother dies during your father's mourning, lay aside father's mourning and put on mourning for her, except when performing sacrifices for father.
items.quote: he put off the mourning for his father (and assumed that proper for his mother).

items.text: If mourning for an uncle or cousin falls during mourning for a parent, do not put off the parent's mourning except for sacrifices for the uncle or cousin; then resume.
items.quote: the previous mourning was not laid aside, save when the sacrificial services in these cases required it

items.text: If your eldest son dies during the three years' mourning for a parent, after assuming the coarser girdle, you may continue the parent's sacrifices.
items.quote: after the coarser girdle of the Kiung hemp had been assumed in the latter case, the sacrifices... might be proceeded with.

items.text: If you hear of a relative's death while another coffin is in the house, go to a separate room to wail, then offer to the primary deceased and wail again.
items.quote: When a mourner, while the coffin was in the house, heard of the death of another relative at a distance, he went to another apartment and wailed for him.

heading: Liji 18 · Za Ji 雜記 · Miscellaneous Records · Za Ji II.i.23 … Za Ji II.i.38

items.text: Offer the prescribed victims at the sacrifice of Repose, at the conclusion of wailing, and at the placing of the spirit-tablet.
items.quote: there were offered a boar and a ram; at the conclusion of the wailing, and at the placing of his spirit-tablet, there was, in addition, the bull.
items.conflict: Offerings to the dead are idolatrous; worship God alone.

items.text: When divining about burial or repose for a father or grandfather, style yourself 'the sorrowing.'
items.quote: A son or grandson spoke of himself as 'the sorrowing,' (when divining about his father or grandfather)
items.conflict: Divination is forbidden (Deut. 18:10-12).

items.text: When consulting the tortoise-shell about your wife's burial or repose, say 'So and so for so and so.'
items.quote: a husband (divining about his wife) said, 'So and so for so and so'
items.conflict: Divination is forbidden (Deut. 18:10-12).

items.text: When divining about a younger brother, simply give your own name.
items.quote: an elder brother about a younger brother, simply said, 'So and so;'
items.conflict: Divination is forbidden (Deut. 18:10-12).

items.text: When divining about an elder brother, say 'For my elder brother, so and so.'
items.quote: a younger brother about an elder brother said, 'For my elder brother, so and so.'
items.conflict: Divination is forbidden (Deut. 18:10-12).

items.text: After sending away the offerings to the dead, wrap up what remains, treating your parents as honored guests.
items.quote: When a son treats his parents in this way as his (honoured) guests, it is an expression of his grief (for their loss).
items.conflict: Offerings to the dead are not Christian practice; the dead cannot receive them.

items.text: If the ruler sends a gift during your three years' mourning, receive it without declining and present it in your ancestral temple.
items.quote: If it came from the ruler with a message from him, he did not presume to decline it;--he received it and presented it (in his ancestral temple).
items.conflict: Presenting gifts in an ancestral temple is ancestor worship; God alone is to be worshiped.

items.text: At the prescribed months of the one-year mourning, put on the lien silk and offer the hsiang and than sacrifices to conclude the mourning.
items.quote: in the thirteenth month they offered the hsiang sacrifice, and in the same month that called than
items.conflict: Rites for the dead are not commanded; trust in Christ alone.

items.text: While in the three years' mourning, do not go to condole with other mourners even if you have occasion, until after you have put on the lien silk.
items.quote: During the mourning for three years, even though they had occasion to assume the dress proper for the nine months' mourning, they did not go to condole

items.text: Enshroud the corpse before putting on the grave-clothes, so that the body is covered.
items.quote: the corpse was first enshrouded, and afterwards came the grave-clothes.
